background.definition: Esophageal varices are dilated portal-systemic collateral blood vessels that develop as a direct result of portal hypertension.

list.listitem: Among patients with cirrhosis without varices, 5% develop varices within 1 year and 28% at 3 years.
Between 5% and 15% of patients with varices develop hemorrhage each year.
In a cohort of 598 patients with hepatitis C and advanced fibrosis, varices developed in 26.2% of patients; only 1% experienced hemorrhage in 4 years.
A similar percentage of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis (20.2%) developed varices by 5 years.
Approximately half of patients with cirrhosis have gastroesophageal varices.
In a cohort of 598 patients with hepatitis C and advanced fibrosis, varices were present in 35.1% of patients; 35.2% had variceal progression or bleeding at 4 years.

In a cohort study of children with biliary atresia, the most common cause of childhood cirrhosis, 125/139 had clinical or ultrasonographic signs of portal hypertension and of these patients, 88 (63%) had esophageal varices, including 74 who were younger than 2 years; in follow-up, eight children had GI bleeding at a median age of 17 months.
Variceal bleeding is expensive to treat; a Portland VA study found that over $1.6 million was required to treat 100 bleeding episodes in 79 patients over a 4-year period.
In a French study, the cost to treat each episode of bleeding was over $14,000, $16,000, and $18,000 for patients with Child Class A, B, and C liver disease, respectively.
Bleeding varices accounts for about 6% of hospital admissions for acute upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding.
Esophageal varices, a manifestation of portal hypertension, are most commonly caused by cirrhosis from alcoholic liver disease and chronic active hepatitis.

Other conditions that cause cirrhosis are primary biliary cirrhosis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, autoimmune hepatitis, chronic hepatitis B, hereditary hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (see Chapter Steatohepatitis (fatty liver)).
Patients with cirrhosis have hepatic fibrosis, distortion of the hepatic architecture, and develop regenerative nodules within the liver which causes portal hypertension.

Esophageal varices are the result of portal hypertension and are almost always associated with a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) greater than or equal to 10 to 12 mm Hg. (Normal is 3-5 mm Hg.)
Elevated pressure in the portal circulation results in the dilation of collateral vessels between the portal and systemic circulation.

Portal pressures are further elevated by two other factors: intrahepatic vasoconstriction due to decreased nitrous oxide production and increased portal blood flow due to splanchnic arteriolar vasodilation.

In 2021 there was an update in Baveno VII concept. They presented criteria for the term liver “recompensation” which was initially observed in cases like delisting from liver transplantation or clinical improvement when the etiological factor for cirrhosis resolved. It has been proposed that portal hypertension could be reversed as part of recompensating liver function, with an undetermined role of non-selective betablockers.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Child's class B or C cirrhosis

list.listitem: Patients should be screened for varices with esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) when the diagnosis of cirrhosis is first made. C
In patients with Child class B or C chronic liver disease and varices, nonselective beta blockers (NSBB) should be used to prevent the first variceal bleed. A
Patients with no history of variceal bleeding who take nonselective beta blockers do not require follow-up EGD. C
Patients with esophageal varices should receive prophylactic treatment: either medical, surgical, or a combination. A
Screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is recommended at the diagnosis of cirrhosis to detect esophageal and gastric varices.
Patients with compensated cirrhosis with no varices should have repeat EGD in 2 to 3 years; those with small varices should have repeat EGD in 1 to 2 years.
Patients with decompensated cirrhosis should have an EGD every year.
Patients with no history of variceal bleeding who are placed on NSBB do not require follow-up EGD.
Predicting esophageal bleeding

Authors of a meta-analysis of studies of liver transient elastography found the test useful for predicting the presence of any esophageal varices (diagnostic o 10; 95% CI 7-14) and large varices (dOR 40; 95% CI 15-107), but there was heterogeneity between studies and evidence of publication bias.dd62

In one study, spleen transient elastography with a cutoff of 55.2 kPa was more useful than liver elastography for predicting variceal bleeding with an area under the curve of 0.92 (95% CI: 0.88-0.97).

Another study predicted high-risk esophageal varices using point shear wave elastography (pSWE) versus 2D shear wave elastography (2D-SWE) to measure the liver and spleen stiffness. Both have good and similar predictive capability with sensitivity 0.91 versus 0.89 and specificity of 0.79 versus 0.72, respectively. However, the area under the curve was higher for pSWE 0.92 than 2D-SWE 0.84.

Validation of the Baveno VI criteria was assessed in a recent study to predict variceal bleeding in 341 patients with HBV decompensated cirrhosis. No patients were missed in the 70 patients with high-risk bleeding in need of EGD.

In a cross-sectional study of non-invasive tests used in the prediction of esophageal varices on 21 Brazilian patients with decompensated cirrhosis caused by non alcoholic fatty liver disease, investigators found that liver stiffness measurement, in particular, spleen diameter to platelet ratio score and varices risk score, enabled sparing 75-80% of EGDs for varices in need of treatment, with area under the curve of 0.96 for detection of variceal bleeding.
Another non-invasive score to predict the esophageal varices is vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) with an AUC of 0.86.

Based on a Cochrane network meta-analysis on the primary prevention of variceal bleeding, the following treatments were associated with lower mortality vs. no active intervention based on low-certainty evidence: beta-blockers, variceal band ligation, sclerotherapy, and beta-blockers plus nitrates. Patients on non-selective beta-blockers, the most commonly used intervention in trials, had a 21.2% mortality during a follow-up period of 8-60 months.

The 2024 AASLD guidelines recommended use of NSBB in primary prevention early especially in Child C patients. In cases of high-risk varices and ascites, they recommended carvedilol as it decreases mortality when compared to endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL). The survival improvement with carvedilol when compared to EVL is 7.8 vs. 4.2 years. In addition, EVL carries a higher risk of complications. They explained that the higher mortality with NSBB observed in previous studies can be attributed to use of high doses of the drug leading to low blood pressure.
In the patient with established esophageal varices, an NSBB (propranolol, nadolol) should be started and adjusted to the maximum tolerated dose.

Among patients with cirrhosis and small varices that have not yet bled, 14% on beta-blockers develop bleeding compared with 30% of control patients. However, in a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs of patients with cirrhosis but no or small varices, use of NSBB did not influence first upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding or death.

Portal vein thrombosis occurs in 20% to 50% of patients with cirrhosis. Authors of a systematic review of 8 studies of patients with cirrhosis and portal vein thrombosis found that use of low-molecular weight heparin or warfarin vs. no therapy improved recanalization with no difference in the proportions of patients with major or minor bleeding between groups (6 studies, 11% in each group) and a reduced rate of spontaneous variceal bleeding (4 studies).

Patients with medium/large varices with high-risk features (Child B/C or red wale markings on endoscopy) who have not bled should receive either nonselective beta-blockers (propranolol or nadolol) or EVL for prevention of first variceal bleed. It is recommended that EVL be repeated at regular intervals until varices are obliterated.

In a meta-analysis of 12 clinical trials including 1023 patients with cirrhosis and varices that have not yet bled, there was a trend favoring EVL for reduced variceal bleeding compared with beta-blockers but no significant difference in gastrointestinal bleeding (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.61, 1.02) or all-cause mortality (RR 1.06; 95% CI 0.86, 1.30).

In a meta-analysis of studies of patients who have had a variceal bleed, combination treatment with an NSBB and EVL was more effective in preventing rebleeding than either beta-blocker monotherapy (37% vs 53%, NNT 7; 95% CI 5, 14) or EVL alone (26% vs 38%, NNT 9; 95% CI 6, 25).

This was confirmed in three more recent meta-analyses one of which also reported reduced mortality rates with combination beta-blocker and endoscopic treatment (either sclerotherapy or band ligation) (OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.03, 1.98).

In secondary prevention of variceal bleeding, authors of a Cochrane network meta-analysis found a greater effect of adding sclerotherapy to nitrates on lowering mortality as compared to: no intervention, portocaval shunts, sclerotherapy alone or band ligation alone, based on moderate-certainty evidence. Mortality following sclerotherapy reached 22.5% in the period of 2-61 months. In addition, variceal band ligation had a lower incidence of adverse events than sclerotherapy (OR 0.19, CI 95% 0.06-0.54). Beta-blockers when added to sclerotherapy caused more serious side effects than beta-blockers alone (OR 2.75, CI 95% 1.18-6.82).

In a meta-analysis comparing EVL with beta-blockers plus isosorbide mononitrate for secondary prevention, there were similar rates of gastrointestinal and variceal bleeding but a lower risk for all-cause deaths in the medical group (RR 1.25; 95% CI 1.01, 1.55).

Portosystemic shunts, including transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS), are more effective in preventing rebleeding than endoscopic therapy (ET; NNT 4; 95% CI 3, 5), however they have previously been associated with a high rate of hepatic encephalopathy (NNH 8; 95% CI 6, 13) and have no beneficial effect on survival. These findings were confirmed in a recent RCT of 72 unselected patients with cirrhosis. However, a similar RCT of 73 Chinese patients with advanced cirrhosis and portal vein thrombosis found lower 2-year rebleeding rates with TIPS than endoscopic band ligation plus propranolol (77.8% vs. 42.9%) without increasing rates of encephalopathy; survival rates were similar.

Cochrane authors also found that, when compared to band ligation, TIPS rerduced rebleeding from esophageal varices (HR 0.12, CI 95% 0.03-0.41). There was uncertainty regarding the effect of the studied interventions on mortality. None of the interventions (i.e.betablockers, nitrates, sclerotherapy, band ligation, portocaval shunt, and TIPS) appeared to be superior to another.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 28 RCTs comparing different procedures for prevention of re-bleeding found no significant differences in overall mortality and 30-day or 6-week survival between surgical portosystemic shunts, TIPS and ET. The authors confirmed that surgical shunts were more effective than either TIPS or ET on re-bleeding without a significant difference in encephalopathy, although there was a trend towards higher incidence of hepatic encephalopathy comparing TIPS and ET.
Devascularization in patients with portal hypertension reduced the rate of hepatic encephalopathy but increased recurrent bleeding compared to use of shunting.

Based on a recent meta-analysis, early TIPS for acute bleeding varices is associated with a decrease in failure of bleeding control with an RR of 0.15 (95% CI, 0.07–0.29) and an improvement in survival for high-risk Child B (RR of 0.53, 95% CI0.31–0.93) and Child C (RR of 0.55, 95% CI 0.37– 0.82) patients with active bleeding.

In a 2020 Cochrane review comparing different surgical shunts to different endoscopic interventions, with and without medical treatment, as a preventive measure for rebleeding (27 RCTs with 1828 participants), there was uncertainty about whether the portosystemic shunts reduced mortality, rebleeding episodes, death caused by rebleeding, or occurrence of chronic encephalopathy, as compared to band ligation or sclerotherapy, with or without an associated medical treatment. However, occlusion of shunts by thrombus was highest with TIPS (47.1%), followed by polytetrafluoroethylene stents (17%), and was least with total shunts (3%); the overall occlusion rate was 37%.
Esophageal varices are asymptomatic until they present as an acute gastrointestinal bleed. C
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is the gold standard for diagnosing esophageal varices.
Capsule endoscopy is almost as accurate as EGD for the diagnosis of esophageal varices. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Epigastric pain worse with food, epigastric fullness, anorexia, nausea, early satiety, reflux
Episodes of emesis/straining while defecating or lifting/coughing/generalized convulsions or other mechanisms to acutely increase intra-abdominal pressure followed by upper GI bleeding
Ascites, abnormal liver function, caput medusae, spider angiomata, jaundice
Abnormal liver function tests, ascites and jaundice typically develop rapidly, hepatomegaly
EGD findings, also typically a coincidental finding on abdominal CT performed for another reason (i.e. acute pancreatitis), liver tests are usually normal or only slightly increased

list.listitem: Esophageal varices are asymptomatic until they present as an acute gastrointestinal bleed.
Among patients with varices, about 80% have peripheral edema, 20% have spider nevi, 50% have jaundice, 60% have encephalopathy, 60% have a palpable spleen, and 80% have ascites.

Laboratory tests that may be useful in predicting varices in patients with liver fibrosis are aspartate transaminase (AST), alanine transaminase (ALT) and platelet count—these three tests, with age, comprise the Fibrosis (FIB)-4. In one study, FIB-4, AST to platelet ratio, AST to ALT ratio and the Lok, and Forns scores (described below) had low to moderate diagnostic accuracy in predicting the presence of varices in liver cirrhosis.
In patients with cirrhosis, a lower platelet count and higher spleen diameter predict esophageal varices. See clinical decision rule.

EGD is the gold standard for diagnosing esophageal varices. Capsule endoscopy has 97% concordance with EGD for the diagnosis of esophageal varices and is a diagnostic option. In one case series, however, sensitivity of capsule endoscopy was not sufficient to replace EGD. Capsule endoscopy, while a useful screen for esophageal varices, also has poor ability to discriminate size.
Conventional two-dimensional ultrasound may be useful in the emergency department setting for determining which patients with UGI bleeding require more urgent endoscopy.
Thrombosis of the portal venous system can be detected by endoscopic ultrasound.

Spleen stiffness as measured by transient elastography (response to compression recorded by ultrasound in this case) may predict the presence, but not the grade of esophageal varices. In one study of patients with cirrhosis from Hep B, a liver stiffness measure X spleen diameter/platelet count was found to be a predictor of high risk esophageal varices.

Computed tomography (CT) for diagnosis of varices in patients with liver cirrhosis was assessed in a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 papers resulting in a sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios of 0.87/0.80/3.67/0.18 for predicting any size varices and 0.87/0.88/7.52/0.12 for predicting high-risk varices. The area under the curve using multi-detector CT was 0.90 and 0.95 for predicting any size and high-risk varices, respectively, and 0.87 and 0.97 using multi-detector CT esophagograms.

Magnetic resonance (MR) elastography was comparable to dynamic contrast material-enhanced MR in detecting hepatic and spleen stiffness and predicting the presence of esophageal varices and high-risk varices.

Hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) is the gradient between pressures in the portal vein and the abdominal portion of the inferior vena cava. A wedged catheter is used to stop blood flow in the hepatic vein creating a proximal static column of blood which transmits the pressure from the hepatic sinusoids to the catheter, similar in concept to a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure measurement. The normal HVPG value is between 1 and 5 mm Hg. This procedure is simple, but invasive.

Based on the Baveno VII consensus in 2021, the AASLD 2024 guidelines endorsed some non-invasive methods for diagnosis of clinically-significant portal hypertension including both the platelet count and liver stiffness as important predictors.

A clinical decision rule based on platelet count and spleen size has been developed and validated to predict the likelihood that a patient with cirrhosis has esophageal varices. It was 100% sensitive and 71% specific in a validation study.A meta-analysis of 20 studies evaluating the platelet count/spleen diameter ratio confirmed its high accuracy in diagnosis of esophageal varices in patients with compensated cirrhosis.

A combination of Lok index (−5.56 − 0.0089 × Platelet (×103/mm3) + 1.26 × AST/ALT ratio + 5.27 × INR; Cutoff = 0.9) and Forns' index (7.811 − 3.131.ln(platelet count) + 0.781.ln(GGT) + 3.467.ln(age) − 0.014.(cholesterol); cutoff = 8.5) predicted presence of any grade of esophageal varices with good performance (AUC 0.82).
An algorithm combining the Lok score, liver and spleen stiffness was useful in identifying patients at low risk of having high-risk esophageal varices.

In a retrospective study of 104 patients with chronic liver disease, the Baveno VI consensus criteria of liver stiffness <20 kPa and platelet count >150,000/ul performed well for ruling out esophageal varices with a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 61.5%.

A model for end-stage liver disease (MELD)-based model was developed that predicts mortality among patients with acute variceal bleeding. For patients with a MELD score (using serum bilirubin, creatinine and INR) of 19 or greater mortality was 20% or greater, whereas MELD scores less than 11 predicted less than 5% mortality.

Among 202 patients with cirrhosis who survived an acute variceal bleed, the MELD-Na (adding serum sodium) and AIMS65 (using albumin, INR, altered mental status, systolic blood pressure, and age over 65 years) scoring systems performed best for predicting 6-week mortality with an area under the curve of 0.781 and 0.808, respectively.

In a retrospective study of 144 adult patients undergoing TIPS for refractory esophageal (79%) or gastric bleeding, 6-week and 12-month mortality was 36% and 42%, respectively. MELD score was predictive of 6-week mortality and Child-Pugh score was predictive of 12-month mortality. For the latter, overall survival was significantly longer in those with Child-Pugh class A/B compared to class C (median survival 334 vs. 48 days.
Suspect variceal bleeding in patients with painless UGI bleeding who have signs of cirrhosis.

Patients with acute variceal bleeding should receive vasopressin analogs; early TIPS also appears to improve outcomes; these drugs do not prevent rebleeding and data are conflicting on mortality reduction. B

Patients with cirrhosis and UGI bleeding should receive prophylactic antibiotics which appear to reduce mortality. However, 2 to 3 days of therapy are likely to be non-inferior compared to longer (5 to 7 days) courses. A
The combination of endoscopic therapy plus medication improves initial hemostasis and hemostasis at 5 days, but has no effect on mortality. A
In the initial control of acute bleeding, EVL is slightly more effective than endoscopic injection sclerotherapy. A

TIPS was superior to medical/endoscopic therapy in decreasing the incidence of treatment failure (OR 0.22; 95% CI, 0.11-0.44), improving overall survival (HR 0.55; 95% CI, 0.38-0.812), and decreasing the incidence of bleeding-related death. B

Based on one RCT, emergency portocaval shunting is better than endoscopic sclerotherapy and rescue portocaval shunt in all outcomes, including 10-year survival. B This finding was confirmed for emergency portocaval shunting over TIPS in a second RCT from the same institution.

In 21 trials with over 2500 patients with acute variceal bleeding, somatostatin and its derivatives did not reduce overall mortality or prevent rebleeding. Overall, patients treated with somatostatin needed about 1/2 unit of packed red cells less than control patients.

In a Cochrane review with over 1600 patients, terlipressin, a synthetic vasopressin analog, reduced total mortality by 34% compared with control patients. With an overall event rate in the control patients of 36% (NNT 9; 95% CI 6 to 298).

Authors of a more recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 RCTs with 3344 patients confirmed that terlipressin was significantly better than placebo for control of bleeding within 48 hours (OR 2.94) and decreased in-hospital mortality (OR 0.31).

In a meta-analysis of 5 trials of patients with initially controlled variceal bleeding, authors found no difference in 5-day rebleeding rate between patients treated with vasopressin/terlipressin or somatostatin/octreotide. In the most recent meta-analysis, complication rates appeared higher with vasopressin vs. terlipressin but were lower comparing somatostatin with terlipressin.
About 18% of patients with cirrhosis and acute UGI bleeding receiving prophylactic antibiotics die compared with 22% of control patients (NNT 20; 95% CI 12, 114).

A 2025 meta-anlalysis of RCT found that a shorter duration of antibiotic prophylaxis (2-3 days), including no prophylaxis, is noninferior to a longer duration of antibiotic prophylaxis (5-7 days) for mortality prevention in patients with cirrhosis who present with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. However, it may lead to a higher incidence of early rebleeds and bacterial infections.

Based on two randomized trials with 493 randomized subjects, authors of a Cochrane review found no evidence to support or reject the administration of human recombinant activated factor VII vs placebo for patients with liver disease and UGI bleeding in reducing mortality; while there was sufficient evidence to exclude a decrease in mortality by 80%, there was insufficient evidence to exclude smaller effects.
While commonly administered to patients with advanced liver disease who have acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, no randomized trials exist to determine whether vitamin K is truly effective.

Based on a Cochrane network meta-analysis (52 RCTs with 4580 participants), the treatment for the bleeding varcies due to decompensated liver cirrhosis includes 19 different interventions. Scelrotherapy, the most common intervention in trials and considered the standard therapy, is associated with a 15.8% mortality. None of the trials reported on quality of life.
In a systematic review of 12 studies with over 1100 patients with acute variceal bleeding, emergency sclerotherapy as the initial intervention was no more effective than vasoactive medications.

In a systematic review of 8 randomized trials with over 500 patients, compared with medication alone, combination therapy with ET plus medication improved initial hemostasis (NNT 8; 95% CI 5, 16) and hemostasis at 5 days (NNT 5; 95% CI 4, 8), but had no effect on mortality. Authors of a systematic review concluded that 3-5 days of adjuvant vasoactive drugs following ET was not superior to a shorter course.

In a systematic review of 10 clinical trials of 404 patients, EVL was slightly more effective than endoscopic injection sclerotherapy in the initial control of bleeding (NNT 16). This finding was confirmed in a meta-analysis of 14 studies.

TIPS is an image-guided procedure that bypasses much of the hepatic circulation by connecting the portal vein to the hepatic vein via a stent using a guidewire introduced through the jugular vein. The procedure is usually performed by interventional radiologists.
TIPS is indicated in patients in whom variceal hemorrhage cannot be controlled or in whom bleeding persists despite endoscopic treatment combined with pharmacologic therapy.
TIPS was better than medical/endoscopic therapy in decreasing treatment failure and improving overall survival in a meta-analysis of 6 studies.

In a small RCT of 49 patients with primarily Child-Pugh class A or B, pulmonary vein thrombosis and variceal bleeding in the past 6 weeks, those randomized to TIPS with a covered stent vs. endoscopic band ligation plus propranolol had a lower rate of rebleeding at 2 years (25% vs. 50%) and higher recanalization rate but no significant differences in survival (67% vs 84%, respectively), overt hepatic encephalopathy (25% vs 16%), or other complications of portal hypertension.

In 4 trials evaluating early TIPS in patients with cirrhosis and acute variceal bleeding, early TIPS was associated with fewer deaths overall but not in patients with Child-Pugh B or C. Early TIPS reduced rebleeding rates without increased rates of encephalopathy.

Surgical shunting includes distal splenorenal shunts (detaching the splenic vein from the portal vein and reattaching it to the left renal vein) and portacaval shunts (connecting the portal vein to the inferior vena cava).

In a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs and one case-control study, surgical shunting performed better than TIPS for bleeding varices for 2-year survival (OR 2.5; 95% CI 1.2, 5.2) and was associated with significantly less frequent shunt failure (OR 0.3; 95% CI 0.1, 0.9).

In a cohort study with 10-year follow-up, emergency portocaval shunting vs. repeat sclerotherapy and rescue shunt resulted in improved outcomes including survival after 5 years (72% vs. 22%), 10 years (46% vs. 16%), and 15 years (46% vs. 0%); incidence of recurrent portal-systemic encephalopathy (15% vs. 43%); and mean quality of life points (lower is better) (13.89 vs. 27.89); direct costs were also lower.

Based on two RCT of patients with bleeding esophageal varices from the same institution noted above, emergency portocaval shunting performed better than emergency endoscopic sclerotherapy or TIPS with respect to permanently controlled bleeding (97%-100% vs. 20% and 22%, respectively), portal-systemic encephalopathy (15% vs. 35% and 61%, respectively) and survival, at lower cost.

Balloon tamponade temporarily controls hemorrhage in over 80% of patients, however lethal complications such as aspiration, necrosis or perforation of the esophagus can occur in up to 20% of patients. Therefore its use should be for temporizing until more definitive therapy (endoscopic therapy or TIPS) can be initiated.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies of self-expanding metal stents in patients with cirrhosis and severe or refractory esophageal variceal bleeding, found stents beneficial, with a pooled estimate rate for death of 0.40 (95% CI, 0.31-0.49). They concluded that stents could be used as a bridge to TIPS or to liver transplantation in a significant proportion of patients.

For patients with unshuntable extra-hepatic portal hypertension and bleeding varices, radical esophagogastrectomy (total gastrectomy and resection of the distal two thirds of the esophagus) was successful with respect to survival without rebleeding in all 44 patients from a single institution; quality of life was rated as good or excellent in 91%.
Patients who are alcoholics should be counseled to avoid alcohol and be referred to alcohol treatment programs.
In a study of adherence to guidelines for first episode of esophageal varices bleeding and outcomes, adherence was better in a specialized unit vs. a community hospital but outcomes were similar.
summarizes the approach to managing the hospitalized patient with acute variceal bleeding.

A non-invasive scoring system for critically-ill patients with suspected esophageal varices has been proposed using a combination of the variceal metric score with the Glasgow Blatchford score (GBS), the latter based on clinical, laboratory and sonographic findings. No patients with a low-risk metric score (0-4 points) and a GBS <2 had esophageal varices. In contrast, patients with high-risk metric scores (9-13) and GBS >2 had a 94% chance of varices and patients with very high metric scores (14-17) all had varices.

listitem.strong: Nasoenteric tube placement can be considered in patients with esophageal varices. As malnutrition and sarcopenia reaches 60 in patients with decompensated cirrhosis, tube placement can help with administration of nutrients and medications, bowel decompression, gastric lavage or decompression, and bowel preparation for endoscopy.

list.listitem: Each episode of variceal bleeding is associated with about a 20% risk of mortality. B
In patients with acute variceal bleeding, the rebleeding risk in untreated patients is 60% within 1 to 2 years of initial bleed. There is also a 33% mortality in untreated variceal bleeds. A
Lowering the hepatic pressure vein gradient (HVPG) by at least 12 mm Hg or by at least 20% is associated with a 60% reduction in mortality and 80% reduction in recurrent bleeding risk. B
Among patients with cirrhosis without varices, 28% develop varices at three years; about 10% of patients with varices will hemorrhage each year.
In patients with acute variceal bleeding, the rebleeding risk in untreated patients is 60% within 1 to 2 years of initial bleed. There is also a 33% mortality in untreated variceal bleeds.
In patients with compensated cirrhosis, those with hepatic pressure vein gradient (HVPG) <10 mm Hg have a 90% probability of not decompensating over a median of 4 years of follow up.
Alcohol-associated cirrhosis, Child's class B or C, and red wale marks at first endoscopic exam were all associated with a greater risk of variceal progression.
Constipation, vomiting, severe coughing, and excessive consumption of alcohol may precipitate rupture of esophageal varices.
Each episode of variceal bleeding is associated with about a 20% risk of mortality.

In 12 studies with over 900 patients, lower hepatic pressure vein gradient (HVPG) was associated with lower risks of bleeding. Lowering the HVPG by at least 12 mm Hg or by at least 20% was associated with a 60% reduction in mortality and 80% reduction in recurrent bleeding risk.

In a meta-analysis of 10 studies with 595 patients who underwent 2 measurements of hepatic pressure vein gradient (HVPG) for monitoring response to pharmacologic therapy, those whose HVPG declined by at least 12 mm Hg or by at least 20% from baseline had the best outcomes. This suggests that HVPG can be used to monitor drug therapy.

In children with extrahepatic portal venous obstruction with variceal bleeding, EVL followed by sclerotherapy resulted in fewer complications (7% vs. 28%) than esophageal sclerotherapy alone; there were fewer gastroesophageal varices on follow-up but similar rates of increased gastric varices and portal hypertensive gastropathy.

cell.label: Patient with newly diagnosed cirrhosis. Perform EGD to screen for varices. Varices present?
Child-Pugh class (B or C; see ) or presence of red wale marks?
Start nonselective beta-blocker and titrate to maximum tolerated dose. Consider endoscopic variceal ligation.
Start nonselective beta-blocker and titrate to maximum tolerated dose OR perform endoscopic variceal ligation.
Child-Pugh class (B or C, see ) or presence of red wale marks?
Start nonselective beta-blocker OR perform follow-up EGD in 2 years if compensated cirrhosis or yearly if decompensated cirrhosis.
Start a nonselective beta-blocker and titrate to maximum tolerated dose. No need to monitor with EGD.

footnotes.footnote: *Management of patients with no prior bleeding.

Data from Garcia-Tsao G, Sanyal AJ, Grace ND, Carey W; Practice Guidelines Committee of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases, Practice Parameters Committee of the American College of Gastroenterology. Prevention and management of gastroesophageal varices and variceal hemorrhage in cirrhosis. Hepatology 2007;46(3):922–938.

cell.label: Assess airway and manage, as indicated; establish IV access; provide volume resuscitation and blood component therapy with a goal hemoglobin of 8 g/dL.

Give somatostatin 250 mcg IV bolus followed by 50 mcg per hour and continue for 3-5 days after blood is diagnosed. (May substitute octreotide, 50 mcg bolus followed by 50 mcg per hour. May alternatively consider vasopressin 0.2 to 0.4 units per minute IV, max dose 0.8 units per minute, with nitroglycerin 40 mcg per minute IV, max dose 400 mcg per minute, for no greater than 24 hours.) DO NOT use beta-blockers acutely.
Admit to ICU. Start oral norfloxacin or IV ciprofloxacin (ceftriaxone 1 g per day may also be used).
Obtain GI consultation within 12 hours. Perform EGD with endoscopic variceal ligation. Consider sclerotherapy if ligation not technically feasible.
If bleeding is not controlled, balloon tamponade or transhepatic intraportal shunt may be performed as rescue therapy.
